extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and editorial commentary aimed at informing the public about global wartime developments and outlining postwar political goals; mixes battlefield dispatches with policy speech excerpts. Focus is on clear factual reporting, attribution of claims, and argumentative policy prescriptions for wartime/postwar conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of the colonial system as a war aim
rubrics_metrics.description: “Freedom means the orderly but scheduled abolition of the colonial system.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that freedom requires replacing colonial systems (regardless of which nation holds them) with arrangements like a Commonwealth of Free Nations; emphasizes this as part of what must be fought for and preserved after victory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep commitments to promised independence
rubrics_metrics.description: “If we fail to deliver, by force of arms, the independence we have promised to the Filipinos, the whole Pacific world will be the loser.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promised independence must be honored promptly because failure undermines strategic and moral interests; delivering clear dates or guarantees gives colonized peoples something to work toward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a patronizing attitude toward non‑Western peoples
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticizes the “half‑ignorant, half‑patronizing way” Americans have treated peoples in eastern Europe and Asia and stresses that allied rulers are "proud and intelligent men."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat leaders such as the Shah of Iran, Prime Ministers of Iraq and Turkey, Generalissimo of China, etc., with respect; recognize their ideas about abolishing imperialism and making freedom a reality rather than speaking down to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send representatives with authority and cultural competence
rubrics_metrics.description: We have “consistently failed to send to these men representatives with authority to discuss such problems intelligently and to take realistic steps toward their solution.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send high‑level, distinguished envoys (cabinet rank where appropriate) who are able to tell national leaders truths and take realistic steps; they should learn languages and be in residence in regions (example: lack of Ministers/Ambassadors in Arab‑speaking areas criticized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wipe out distinction between first‑class and second‑class allies
rubrics_metrics.description: “We must wipe out the distinction in our minds between ‘first‑class’ and ‘second‑class’ allies.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat all allies and potential allies as equals and send representatives of sufficient stature to engage them respectfully and effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit censorship; publish factual information subject only to military security
rubrics_metrics.description: “Facts should not be censored. They should be given to us all. For unless we recognize and correct [them] we may lose the friendship ... A misdirected censorship will not accomplish this.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opposes arbitrary or undemocratic censorship that atrophies intelligence; facts about war performance and resource use should reach the public except where genuine military security requires restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage public criticism and democratic scrutiny of experts
rubrics_metrics.description: “Military experts, as well as our leaders, must be constantly exposed to democracy’s greatest driving power—the whiplash of public opinion... Men with great power usually like to live free of criticism. But when they get that way, that’s the time to increase the criticism.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public criticism can correct mistakes (example: changes in North Africa command after criticism); citizens (including non‑experts) should not be silenced from suggesting improvements to military, industrial, economic, or political conduct of the war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan now for peace on a global basis
rubrics_metrics.description: “First, we must plan now for peace on a global basis ... it must embrace the earth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postwar planning should be global rather than local — peace must secure foundations everywhere (political and economic); continents and oceans are interconnected, and there can be no durable peace for part of the world alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure freedom includes economic as well as political dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: “The world must be free, economically and politically, for nations and for men that peace may exist in it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peoples seek freedom not only for political satisfaction but for economic advancement; postwar policy should support economic opportunity and cooperation enabling peoples to address their own problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: America must play an active, constructive part in creating and keeping peace
rubrics_metrics.description: “Third, America must play an active, constructive part in freeing it and keeping its peace.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. should be a confident partner in building a new global society, using its resources and influence now (not only after the war) to promote liberty and justice and to help create institutions for postwar order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge differing readiness for independence and provide guarantees/timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: “Not all the peoples of the world are ready for freedom, or can defend it, the day after tomorrow. But today they all want some date to work toward, some guaranty that the date will be kept.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that immediate self‑government may not be feasible everywhere; provide credible timelines or guarantees so peoples can prepare and cooperate economically and politically to assume independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use U.S. giving/aid power promptly to promote liberty and justice
rubrics_metrics.description: “They expect us now — not after the war — to use the enormous power of our giving to promote liberty and justice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humanitarian and reconstruction aid should be deployed during and immediately after the war to strengthen partners, promote justice, and support the new global order the speech advocates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume the infallibility of military/naval experts
rubrics_metrics.description: “The record of this war to date is not such as to inspire in us any sublime faith in the infallibility of our military or naval experts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers and the public should remain skeptical and keep experts accountable; historical examples (e.g., Maginot) show that leaving all decisions to experts can produce grave mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report and attribute opposing claims transparently in battlefield dispatches
rubrics_metrics.description: News text repeatedly presents both Allied and Axis communiqués and notes conflicting claims (e.g., prisoner counts, tanks destroyed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting military actions, attribute claims to their sources (Allied communiqués, Axis broadcasts, etc.), present counterclaims, and note when details are unconfirmed so readers can judge reliability.
